references.text: Jesus' words in the Sermon on the Mount about disciples being the salt of the earth, with a warning that salt which loses its flavor is good for nothing ([ref:Matt 5:13|Matthew 5:13]). This is the parallel passage to Luke 14:34 and contains the same imagery and warning.

Mark's version of Jesus' words about salt: "Salt is a good thing, but if the salt loses its saltiness, what will you use to season it?" ([ref:Mark 9:50|Mark 9:50]). A close parallel with the same message about the value of salt and the loss of its power.

"For everyone will be salted with fire" ([ref:Mark 9:49|Mark 9:49]). In Mark's context, salt is linked to discipleship and sacrifice, which aligns with Luke 14:34 where the saying about salt comes right after the call to carry one's cross.

Paul urges that "your speech should always be gracious, seasoned with salt" ([ref:Kol 4:6|Colossians 4:6]). Here salt is used as a metaphor for what adds flavor and preserves quality, related to Jesus' use of the salt metaphor.

The command that "the salt of your covenant" must not be lacking from grain offerings ([ref:3 Mos 2:13|Leviticus 2:13]). In the Old Testament, salt was connected with covenants and sacrifices, forming the background for Jesus' imagery about the indispensability of salt.

An "everlasting covenant of salt" for Aaron and his descendants ([ref:4 Mos 18:19|Numbers 18:19]). Salt symbolizes the permanence and unchangeableness of the covenant, which deepens the understanding of why salt that loses its flavor is such a serious image.

In Ezekiel's vision of the healing waters, the swamps and marshes are not healed but "given over to salt" ([ref:Esek 47:11|Ezekiel 47:11]). Salt can also represent destruction and judgment, a background that enriches the understanding of Jesus' warning about useless salt.

The verse that follows directly: tasteless salt is good neither for soil nor for fertilizer, but is thrown out ([ref:Luk 14:35|Luke 14:35]). The completion of the image begun in verse 34 – the consequences of losing one's effectiveness as a disciple.
